sections.title: Introduction: The Smoothie Analogy (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the concept of decomposition. Just as a smoothie can be deconstructed back into its original fruit ingredients (strawberries, bananas, blueberries), a complex signal can be broken down into simple sine waves. Define the core objective: transforming data from the Time Domain to the Frequency Domain.
sections.example: A chef blending fruits to create a smoothie; the Fourier Transform acts as the 'inverse blender' that tells you exactly how many grams of each fruit were used.

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Language of Sine Waves (0:45-1:45)
sections.content: Briefly review the parameters of a sine wave: Amplitude, Frequency, and Phase. Visualize these as rotating vectors (phasors) on a complex plane. This builds the foundational mental model for adding multiple waves together to create complex patterns (Superposition Principle).
sections.example: A visual animation showing three simple sine waves of different frequencies stacking up to form a complex 'sawtooth' wave.

sections.title: The Core Concept: The Rotating Windmill (1:45-3:15)
sections.content: Explain the Fourier Transform as a mathematical 'sieve'. We multiply the signal by complex exponentials (rotating vectors) at different frequencies. When the 'rotation speed' matches a frequency hidden in the signal, the signal 'aligns' (constructive interference), creating a peak in the spectrum.
sections.example: An animation of a 'spirograph' drawing: The signal wraps around a center point. If the winding frequency matches the signal frequency, the center of gravity shifts away from the origin, revealing the hidden component.

sections.title: The Result: The Frequency Spectrum (3:15-4:15)
sections.content: Explain the transition from a wave-form (Time Domain) to a 'Bar Chart' (Frequency Domain). Discuss how the peaks in the spectrum represent the 'DNA' of the signal, allowing us to filter noise or compress files.
sections.example: An audio signal of a cat meowing. Show the messy wave in the time domain, then animate it snapping into a neat set of distinct bars on a frequency plot.

sections.title: Conclusion & Real-World Application (4:15-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize how this transformation allows us to manipulate signals—like removing high-frequency hiss from old recordings or compressing images (JPEG). End with the 'big picture': Everything in the universe is just a sum of vibrations.
sections.example: A smartphone using Fourier Transform to perform 'Shazam'—identifying a song by matching its unique frequency fingerprint against a database.
